issues.legal_issue: A compromise decree for eviction is invalid when the court passes it without finding that a statutory ground for eviction exists.
material_facts: The landlord brought an eviction suit alleging residential need, the tenant’s ownership of suitable alternative accommodation, and rent default.
After issues were framed, the parties filed a compromise providing for eviction after a specified date and fixing the rent.
The court passed a decree in accordance with the compromise without recording that any statutory ground for eviction existed.
The tenant later challenged the decree’s validity in execution proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The decree was a nullity insofar as it directed delivery of possession and could not be executed; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 forbids a court from passing an eviction decree unless it is satisfied that a statutory ground for eviction exists. A decree passed without that satisfaction is a nullity and cannot be enforced in execution. The Court followed Bahadur Singh v. Muni Subrat Dass, which applied this principle to a decree passed in terms of an award.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding to evict a tenant from rented premises subject to statutory rent-control restrictions.
predicates.compromise_based_eviction_decree: The court passed an eviction decree in accordance with an agreement between the landlord and tenant.
predicates.no_judicial_finding_of_permitted_evictio: The court did not find that a statutory ground permitting eviction existed.

issues.definition: When a court in a rent-control eviction proceeding decrees eviction by compromise without finding a permitted ground for eviction, the decree is a nullity and cannot be executed.
